1.pericope_label: The twelve sent out with power; Herod perplexed

schools.summary: Note the textual point on the staff, since the better manuscripts give the singular and the plural was probably adopted to harmonise this verse with the other two Gospels. On the dust, prefer a testimony unto them to a testimony against them, while granting that Luke's preposition and Mark's dative come to much the same thing. Give the rabbinic background to the single garment: some clothed themselves so out of religious severity, and the priests went barefoot on the pavement in one garment only — which softens a prohibition that would otherwise look hard with winter coming on. On Herod, mark that the verb for his perplexity is found only in Luke's writings, that the three rumours are reported in the aorist rather than the pluperfect the English suggests, and that the expectation of a risen prophet, though no prophet but Elias was looked for before the Messiah, was common in ordinary talk.

Take the kingdom preached as two things at once, the kingdom of grace set up in men's hearts and the kingdom of glory they are made meet for. Then keep the details concrete: it was the other nine besides the three who had been with him at the raising of Jairus's daughter; the circuit was through the towns and cities of Judea; and the lodging rule concerned the houses they entered for the sake of a night's shelter. On Herod, note that he had ordered the beheading and had proof of it, the head having been brought him in a charger.

Press the pairing in the commission, since Luke names both demons and diseases and prescribes different treatments for each — the demons cast out, the diseases healed — so that either the Evangelist was mistaken or the two are not the same thing. Then give the verb for Herod's perplexity its picture: it is a traveller's word, a man at a meeting of roads only one of which leads where he means to go. And say what put him there, since a guilty conscience is a continual pest and he had murdered John and now feared he should rise and bring the deeds to light.

Explain why the twelve were sent at all: Christ could be in only one place at a time, and they were by now able to deliver what they had received. Take the power over all devils as a design of total ruin against the kingdom of darkness, and note that the healing made them welcome everywhere, convincing judgements and gaining affections together. On the travel rules, teach dependence on Providence but be honest that Paul saw cause not to follow them, labouring with his hands rather than be burdensome. And on the dust shaken off, make it a binding over to the judgement of God, so that those who perish in their unbelief leave their blood on their own heads.

Give three reasons for the stripped equipment rather than one: it rendered the disciples unsuspected, it held them clear of all care so that they might give their whole study to the word, and it taught them their own proper virtue. Then raise the obvious objection yourself — why no scrip, no second coat, no staff — and answer that Christ meant to rouse them to diligence by taking them from the cares of this life. On Herod, mark the delay before he took any notice at all, which shows the pride of a tyrant.

Treat the miracles as credentials. It was fitting that men appointed to holy teaching should be able to work them and be believed ministers of God by those acts themselves; and in giving power over all the devils Christ brought down the haughty pride of the one who had said that there is none who shall open his mouth against him.

Use the passage where it does most work, against those who would sever the gospel from the Creator. Who but the God who feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers of the field would command men to take nothing for the journey, and who but the one who forbade muzzling the treading ox, on the principle that the worker is worthy of his hire? A heretic may expunge such precepts, but the sense of them survives. And do not soften the shaking of the dust: nobody bears witness except where a case is decided by process, so that one who orders conduct to be submitted to testimony is threatening as a judge. The very rumours about who he was attest that no new god was being recommended.

debates.question: Is the dust shaken off a testimony against them, or unto them?

sides.position: Unto them — a testimony borne to them rather than against them
Against them, and judicially so: no one bears witness except where a case is decided by process, so ordering this is to threaten as a judge
The distinction is slighter than it looks; Luke's preposition and Mark's dative come to the same idea

debates.question: Are the demons and the diseases two things or one?

sides.position: Two, and the text proves it: Luke names both and assigns different treatments, the demons cast out and the diseases healed
The distinction cannot be pressed from the vocabulary, since Luke uses two different verbs for healing within a line, apparently interchangeably

outliers.note: Alone raises a difficulty of season, that by his reckoning winter was coming on when the twelve were sent, so that forbidding a second garment seems hard; and alone answers it from rabbinic sources, citing a severity by which some wore one garment only, R. Jose on righteous men dying of a disease of the bowels brought on by such austerity, and the priests who walked barefoot on the pavement clad in a single garment.

Alone reads the whole passage as an argument against Marcion, turning each detail into evidence that the God who gave these commands is the Creator — the one who feeds the ravens, clothes the flowers, and forbade the muzzling of the treading ox — and adding that the very rumours reported to Herod show that no new god was being announced.

Alone gives a threefold reason for the travel rules rather than a single one, and alone frames Herod's slowness to notice as a study in character, since it was long before he took any account of what was being done, which shows the pride of a tyrant.

themes: Then he called his twelve disciples together, and gave them power and authority over all devils, and to cure diseases.
And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, and to heal the sick.
And he said unto them, Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece.
And whatsoever house ye enter into, there abide, and thence depart.
And whosoever will not receive you, when ye go out of that city, shake off the very dust from your feet for a testimony against them.
And they departed, and went through the towns, preaching the gospel, and healing every where.
Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead;
And of some, that Elias had appeared; and of others, that one of the old prophets was risen again.
And Herod said, John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him.

10.pericope_label: The apostles return; five thousand fed in a desert place

schools.summary: Keep the tenses visible, since they carry the scene: he kept on speaking and kept on healing, the breaking of the loaves is a single aorist act and the giving an imperfect, so that Christ broke once and went on giving. Note that Luke, like Matthew, softens Mark's flat five thousand with an about; that the word for the companies means a row of people reclining at a meal and is found nowhere else in the New Testament; and that the noun for healing is not built on the verb translated healed but is a more technical word, close to our treatment, used by Luke almost alone.

Mark the change in the disciples rather than only the miracle: having disputed the case, they stopped and did as they were told, ranging the crowd in companies on the green grass. And say plainly what the apostles had been doing — going through the several parts of the land where they were sent, preaching and working miracles, and finishing the circuit before they returned.

Count the effects of grace in these two verses and let the list do the work: the people are drawn to follow, kindly received, instructed in the things of God, healed of their diseases, and fed in body and soul. Then take the breaking of the loaves as a pattern for ministers, who should exhort the people to hear with reverence, take the bread of life themselves before feeding others, lift the soul often to God, divide rightly the word of truth into portions suited to each capacity, and employ the talents of others for what they cannot do alone.

Draw the rest out of the retreat: he who appointed the man-servant and the maid-servant to rest would have his own servants rest too, and those in the most public stations must sometimes go aside, both to recruit their bodies and to furnish their minds for further work. Then let the interruption teach its own lesson, that pious zeal may excuse a little rudeness, as it did with Christ; and note that the place was no desert where Christ was. On the reporting, observe that they told him all they had done as servants sent on an errand should, so that anything done amiss might be mended next time.
Take the order to sit down as a lesson in hospitality: when we entertain anyone we ought to seat him and give him every comfort.

State the impossibility before the miracle, since it is the point of the exchange: the command to feed them was one the disciples simply could not obey, having no more than five loaves and two fishes between them. And read the withdrawal morally — that Christ hates men of blood and those who keep company with them while they will not leave off their crimes, and so departed after the Baptist's murder.

Ask who the heavenly nourishment is given to, and answer by exclusion: not to the indolent, not to those of rank in the synagogue or in high secular office, not to those in a city, but to those who seek Christ in the desert. Note also, as a matter of arrangement, that Matthew and Mark take occasion here to relate the death of John, which Luke had already given long before, so that he can pass straight from Herod's perplexity to the apostles' return. And in the receiving of the weary, the teaching of the ignorant, the curing of the sick and the filling of the hungry, see the evidence that their devotion pleased him.

outliers.note: Alone addresses the arrangement of the Gospels rather than the meaning of the passage, observing that Matthew and Mark take the occasion here to relate how John was killed, while Luke, having given that account long before, passes directly from Herod's perplexity to the return of the apostles.

Alone asks who the miracle is for and answers by exclusion, denying the nourishment of heavenly grace to the indolent, to men of rank in the synagogue or in high secular office, and to those in a city, and granting it to those who seek Christ in the desert.

Alone turns the whole sequence into a manual for ministers, drawing five duties from the manner of the breaking of the loaves — and counts five effects of grace in the reception of the crowd, both lists taken over from Quesnel.

themes: And the apostles, when they were returned, told him all that they had done. And he took them, and went aside privately into a desert place belonging to the city called Bethsaida.
And the people, when they knew it, followed him: and he received them, and spake unto them of the kingdom of God, and healed them that had need of healing.

And when the day began to wear away, then came the twelve, and said unto him, Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place.
But he said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they said, We have no more but five loaves and two fishes; except we should go and buy meat for all this people.
For they were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, Make them sit down by fifties in a company.
And they did so, and made them all sit down.
Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and brake, and gave to the disciples to set before the multitude.
And they did eat, and were all filled: and there was taken up of fragments that remained to them twelve baskets.

18.pericope_label: Whom say ye that I am: the Christ of God, and the passion foretold

schools.summary: Notice what Luke omits here — the walking on the water, the four thousand, the woman of Canaan, the leaven — and do not explain it too confidently; the likeliest account is that he did not learn these things in the course of his inquiries, from which follows the inference that he had not seen the other two Gospels in the form we have them. Take the stress on the prayer as deliberate, as though what follows were its result. Handle the apparent contradiction between his praying alone and the disciples being with him honestly: either the being alone governs the whole, or a variant reading means that they fell in with him while he prayed. On the confession, mark the emphatic pronoun, and note that the exact phrase, the Christ of God, is peculiar to Luke and answers to the Lord's Christ in Simeon's song.

Say for whom he prayed, since it matters: as man and as mediator. And on the charge of silence, note the order of events — he approved the confession and pronounced Peter blessed, declaring that flesh and blood had not revealed it, before laying the strict command on them. Then let the passion foretold be particular rather than general: the suffering was to be borne in person and character, in soul and body, at the hands of God and men and devils alike.

Keep to what the text will bear and note the variant, that the Coptic and later Persic read the confession as Thou art Christ God. Take the question as addressed to the common people, the mass of them, rather than to any select group.

Make the setting the lesson. Christ found time to be alone though he had much public work; when alone he was praying; his disciples were with him, so this was a family prayer, and householders and parents and masters ought to pray with those under them; and he prayed with them before he examined them, so that the prayer might direct and encourage their answer. On the opinions, observe that the people would make him anything but what he was, and draw the pastoral consequence, that ministers who conversed more with ordinary people would know better how to fit instruction to them, since the more a physician is with his patient the better he knows what to do.

Read the retirement as deliberate instruction: Christ ordained himself an example by an easy method of teaching, since those who rule a people ought to surpass them in good deeds, holding converse with them in all necessary things and treating of those things in which God delights.

Give the opinions their weight — John the Baptist, whom they knew to have been beheaded; Elias, whom they expected; one of the old prophets risen — and then refuse the inquiry itself. To sift such opinions belongs to a different kind of wisdom; for if it was enough for the Apostle Paul to know nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified, what more can anyone desire to know than Christ?

outliers.note: Alone treats Luke's omissions here as evidence about the composition of the Gospels, suggesting that he simply did not learn these facts in the course of his inquiries and inferring that he had not seen Matthew and Mark in the form we now have them.

Alone states what Peter's confession is and is not: not a fresh discovery but the settled conviction of the disciples, held through the defection of the Galilean crowds and the hostility of the Jerusalem authorities, their view of the Messiah still faulty but their loyalty clear — and there was comfort in that for Jesus. He alone also gives the reason for the silence, that the title carried a political meaning which would have led to revolution.
Alone declines the whole question the passage raises, holding that to sift the opinions of the multitude belongs to another kind of wisdom than his, since what sufficed Paul must suffice him.

themes: And it came to pass, as he was alone praying, his disciples were with him: and he asked them, saying, Whom say the people that I am?
They answering said, John the Baptist; but some say, Elias; and others say, that one of the old prophets is risen again.
He said unto them, But whom say ye that I am? Peter answering said, The Christ of God.
And he straitly charged them, and commanded them to tell no man that thing;
Saying, The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day.

23.pericope_label: If any man will come after me, let him take up his cross daily

schools.summary: The disputed word is daily. Report honestly that it is missing from many reputable manuscripts and versions and absent from both parallels, then make the case for keeping it, since it is peculiar to Luke here and the tenses divide the labour — the taking up an aorist, the following a present, so a man takes up his cross and then keeps on following. Note that the address is to all rather than the disciples only, that the sayings which follow are cast throughout in mercantile terms, and that the two verbs about losing should be separated, the first a direct act of self-destruction and the second the forfeiture of something precious. Observe finally that the glory named as Christ's own, alongside the Father's, is peculiar to Luke's report.

Insist that the damage in view is spiritual, and say why the qualification is needed: temporal loss of any kind might be amply compensated by gaining the world, but a hurt to the soul in the smallest degree could not be indemnified by possessing the universe, since earthly goods repair earthly losses and cannot repair a breach in the peace or holiness of the soul.

Take the promise at the end strictly, and let the grammar of it be felt: the double negative and the figure of tasting death are both rabbinical, and like a physician Christ tasted death that we might see how to die. On the following, guard against a crude sense — coming after him cannot mean following his body, which is impossible now that he is in heaven, but a due imitation of his life according to each man's capacity.

Open with the military figure, because it governs the passage. Mighty generals encourage trained soldiers not only by promising the honours of victory but by telling them the suffering itself brings glory, since no man wins fame in battle without taking wounds, and the wound bears witness to the courage of his mind. Then give the occasion: Christ had just told the disciples he must endure the malice of the Jews and be killed and rise, and he adds this lest they suppose he would suffer for the life of the world while they lived quietly and avoided suffering without blame.

Read the not tasting of death strictly rather than as a figure. Those who can stand where Christ is will not experience even the slightest perception of death, and what is denied here is not the death of the body but of the soul. And take the cross named in the verse as the one already spoken of, borne after a Lord who bore his own.

debates.question: Should 'daily' be retained in the text?

sides.position: It is doubtful: missing from many reputable manuscripts, versions and fathers, and absent from the parallels in Matthew and Mark
It is genuine and is the point of the verse, peculiar to Luke in this incident, and matched by a present tense for the following

outliers.note: Alone reports that the word rendered daily is wanting in many reputable manuscripts, versions and fathers, and alone notes that it has no counterpart in either parallel account.

Alone presses the promise about not tasting death into a literal claim, that those united to Christ will not experience even the slightest perception of it, and that the death denied is the soul's and not the body's.

themes: And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.
For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.
For what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away?
For whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he shall come in his own glory, and in his Father’s, and of the holy angels.
But I tell you of a truth, there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the kingdom of God.

28.pericope_label: The transfiguration: this is my beloved Son, hear him

schools.summary: Two things are worth showing from the Greek. Luke avoids the verb the other Evangelists use for the change, and the likeliest reason is that its associations had been fixed by Ovid's great poem on the metamorphoses of pagan legend — a caution natural in the Evangelist with the most classical culture. And the word for the departure is remarkable both for being uncommon in that sense and for covering resurrection and ascension as well as death; press it into the figure it invites, that Moses had led the exodus out of Egypt and Jesus was about to accomplish the exodus of God's people into the promised land on high. Locate the mountain as probably Hermon, note that the purpose of the ascent, to pray, is Luke's own addition, and that Luke alone names the subject of the conversation.

Read the whole scene as proof offered to the eye, since having told the disciples the mystery of his coming, Christ proceeds from words to works and shows them the image of his kingdom. Then distinguish the two kinds of praying: a servant prays by lifting his mind to God, but the mind of Christ, united to God, prayed in order to lead us by the hand up that ascent and to teach that he is not opposed to the Father but reverences him as his beginning. Sum the verse in a phrase — prayer is the revelation of divine glory. On the sleeping, be blunt: Peter was weak and did what is natural to a man.

Make the ascent a lesson in posture: those who look for the fruit of the resurrection and would see the King in his glory must keep the dwelling place of their hearts on high and be always at prayer. Then make the brightness a measure of the beholder — the word is lessened or increased according to your capacity, and unless you climb to a higher wisdom you do not see what glory is in it, the garments of the Word being the discourses of Scripture, so that as the raiment shone the sense of the divine words grows clear. On the sleeping be generous: the brightness of the divine nature overwhelms our bodily senses, since an eye cannot hold even the sun's ray, and perhaps they were weighed down so as to see the sight after rest, a figure of the resurrection. But add the sting — no one sees the glory of Christ except he is watching. And use the presence of Moses and Elias against any who would sever the gospel from the Law and the Prophets: this is how he destroys them, by irradiating them with his glory.

outliers.note: Alone turns the presence of Moses and Elias into an argument, asking why one who came to destroy the Law and the Prophets should exhibit them on the mountain, in conversation with him, and associated in his glory — and answering that this is how he destroys them, by irradiating them with his glory, since nothing could better befit the Creator's Christ than to be seen with those to whom he had appeared and speaking with those who had spoken of him.

Alone supplies the Jewish traditions a first-century reader would have brought to the two figures: that Moses should come with Elias, that Moses was raised alongside Samuel by the witch of Endor, and that Moses did not die but went up into the highest to minister before God.

Alone distinguishes the prayer of a servant from the prayer of Christ, and alone brings in the old image of the hook hidden under the bait, the tyrant who had deceived man with the hope of divinity being himself caught by the clothing of humanity.

Independently of Robertson, and naming the same book, explains Luke's avoidance of the word transfigured by the associations Ovid had fastened on it — a convergence of two commentators from different centuries on the same literary caution.

themes: And it came to pass about an eight days after these sayings, he took Peter and John and James, and went up into a mountain to pray.
And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glistering.
And, behold, there talked with him two men, which were Moses and Elias:
Who appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.
But Peter and they that were with him were heavy with sleep: and when they were awake, they saw his glory, and the two men that stood with him.

And it came to pass, as they departed from him, Peter said unto Jesus, Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias: not knowing what he said.
While he thus spake, there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud.
And there came a voice out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him.
And when the voice was past, Jesus was found alone. And they kept it close, and told no man in those days any of those things which they had seen.

37.pericope_label: The only child with a dumb spirit, and a faithless generation

schools.summary: Draw the small chronological point out of a phrase that is Luke's alone: that it happened on the next day shows the transfiguration took place in the night before. Note that the verbs for coming down and for meeting are, with one exception each, confined to Luke's writings; that the verb the father uses for looking upon his son is one the medical writers employ for examining a patient carefully; that the adverb for the suddenness is theirs too, used of the abrupt onset of diseases such as epilepsy; and that Luke alone calls the boy an only child, as he alone does at Nain. Note also what is missing — the question about the coming of Elijah, which the other two Gospels record here — and account for it by the readership, since among Gentiles there was no such expectation to correct.

Show that the language of the seizure is not a Christian coinage but the ordinary speech of pagan writers for supernatural influence, and prove it from Herodotus: when Scyles the Scythian king was being initiated privately into the Bacchic mysteries, a Borysthenian told the Scythian army that they mocked the Greeks for saying the god possesses us, and yet the same power had now taken possession of their own king. The historian uses the very verb the Evangelist uses, a demon is the agent in both accounts, and both prove the possession real by its effects — the king raging, the boy crying out, convulsed and foaming.

Do not spare the father: his faith was much weakened, as his own words elsewhere show, help thou my unbelief, and if thou canst. And ask why the cure was not simply commanded, answering that Christ made the sufferings public on purpose, bringing those weak in faith to the sight of what was before them; so that when the devil threw the child down and tore him, the order was deliberate — the affliction shown first, the remedy applied after.

Read the descent as part of the design, on the principle that certain places accord with certain events: on the mountain Christ prays and is transfigured and opens the secrets of his glory, and coming down to the lower parts he is met by a crowd; above, the voice of the Father is made known, below, the evil spirits are expelled.

outliers.note: Alone establishes from a pagan historian that the phrase for the seizure was the ordinary Greek for supernatural possession, quoting at length Herodotus on Scyles the Scythian king and the Bacchic mysteries, and observing that the same verb, the same agent and the same proof from effects appear in both writers.
Alone reads the movement of the narrative as structural, setting the mountain against the plain: above, the voice of the Father is made known; below, the evil spirits are expelled.

themes: And it came to pass, that on the next day, when they were come down from the hill, much people met him.
And, behold, a man of the company cried out, saying, Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child.
And, lo, a spirit taketh him, and he suddenly crieth out; and it teareth him that he foameth again, and bruising him hardly departeth from him.
And I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not.
And Jesus answering said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you, and suffer you? Bring thy son hither.
And as he was yet a coming, the devil threw him down, and tare him. And Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and healed the child, and delivered him again to his father.

43.pericope_label: Amazed at the mighty power of God; the saying hid from them

schools.summary: Two points of wording repay attention. The noun for what the crowd wondered at is unusual, appears again in the second epistle of Peter in close connection with the transfiguration, and is elsewhere rendered majesty and magnificence — greatness is perhaps the best equivalent, Luke describing the emotion easterners feel when they say that God is great. And the English rendering of the charge has no word answering to sink: the verb means put, and the emphatic pronoun makes it do you yourselves, whatever others may do, put these words into your ears. Register also that the verse division here is unfortunate and the new paragraph should begin with the words about their wondering; and that the concealment which follows is reported by Luke alone, in a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament, whose clause of purpose at least relieves the disciples of full responsibility for their ignorance.

Say which sayings are meant: not the words already spoken but the prediction about to follow. And locate the obstacle to understanding precisely — they could not reconcile a betrayal and a death with the notions they held of a temporal redeemer and a victorious Messiah.

Take the charge as a rule of attention. Other words may be given occasional hearing, but what concerns his sufferings and death must always be listened to and must occupy a constant place in serious meditation; in joy, remember the cross, our Lord wisely balancing praise with suffering.

Explain why the saying is addressed to the disciples and not to the crowd. Everything Jesus did claimed the admiration of all, but he had just shown his glory on the mountain and delivered a man from an evil spirit, and now the passion had to be faced, so that his disciples might well have asked whether they had been deceived in thinking him God. That is why they are told to lay the saying up as a deposit — and the pronoun distinguishes them, since the multitude were not to know he was about to suffer but were to be assured instead that the dead would rise.

debates.question: What are the sayings to be laid up?

sides.position: Not the words already spoken but the prediction of the passion about to follow
Probably the sayings of the people, who had glorified God at the miracle and so acknowledged him — evidence to be remembered when he was dead and they were doubtful whether he was the Christ

outliers.note: Alone turns the hiding of the saying into a rule for reading Scripture, insisting that it was not God's doing but their own previous false belief, and generalising without hedging that the plainest truths of the Bible are unintelligible to many because they have already embraced an erroneous opinion they are unwilling to abandon.
Alone complains of the printers, holding the verse division at this point singularly unfortunate and the new paragraph properly beginning with the words about their wondering.

themes: And they were all amazed at the mighty power of God. But while they wondered every one at all things which Jesus did, he said unto his disciples,
Let these sayings sink down into your ears: for the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men.
But they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them, that they perceived it not: and they feared to ask him of that saying.

46.pericope_label: Who should be greatest; he that is not against us is for us

schools.summary: Reconstruct the scene from the three accounts together — the disciples in a circle, the child taken to himself and then set at his side rather than in his arms or in the midst as the others have it — and correct the verb, which is rather laid hold on than took. Then find the sharpest thing in the pericope in a variant: the better manuscripts do not read that the least shall be great but that he is great, so the greatness is not deferred as a compensation in some far-off future but attained now, in the midst of the seeming humiliation and by means of it. On the rebuke to John, note the conative imperfect — they tried to hinder rather than succeeded — and the present imperative in reply, stop hindering him; and do not spare the disciple, since the man was doing the Master's work in the Master's name and with the Master's power and merely did not run with the Twelve.

Say how the dispute was known: it happened on the road, behind Christ and out of his hearing, and he perceived it not by any word he had heard but as the omniscient God who is the discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. And guard the child from sentimentality — likeness to it is not in age but in meekness and humility, in not being proud or ambitious of worldly honour or envious of another's better place.

Let the incident of the stranger teach toleration by way of wonder rather than rebuke: marvel at the power of Christ, whose grace works through the unworthy and through those who are not his disciples, as men are sanctified through priests who are not themselves holy.

Treat the dispute as a case of tactics. The devil lays plots of various kinds against those who love the best way of life, sharpening the love of pleasure where he can take a heart by carnal allurement, and where a man has escaped that snare exciting in him a desire of glory instead. Then read the wording as a kindness: to think such thoughts belongs to one who wants to be above the rest, and since it is improbable that all the disciples gave way, the Evangelist's indefinite phrase seems framed on purpose to avoid laying the charge against any individual.
Be gentle with John rather than severe: he loved much and was much beloved, and only thought that those who did not practise obedience should be shut out from the privilege.

outliers.note: Alone reads the Evangelist's indefinite wording as a deliberate charity, arguing that since it is improbable all the disciples gave way to the desire of glory, the phrase about a reasoning arising among them was framed so as not to lay the charge against any one of them.

Alone rests the point of the pericope on a manuscript variant, that the better copies read the least among you is great rather than shall be great, so that the greatness is attained in the humiliation itself rather than deferred as a compensation.

Alone reads John's interruption psychologically, as an attempt to change the subject after the embarrassment of the rebuke, and calls it a pitiful specimen of partisan narrowness and pride even in the Beloved Disciple, one of the sons of thunder.

themes: Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest.
And Jesus, perceiving the thought of their heart, took a child, and set him by him,
And said unto them, Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great.
And John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and we forbad him, because he followeth not with us.
And Jesus said unto him, Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us.

51.pericope_label: He stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem

schools.summary: The word for the receiving up carries the passage. It is old enough to be found in Hippocrates but stands here alone in the New Testament, is derived from the verb used of the Ascension, and shows that Jesus was fully conscious how near his death was. Note the emphatic pronoun in the setting of the face, an idiom found nine times in Ezekiel, the verb itself meaning to fix or make fast; the same look is remarked later by Mark. Observe too that Samaria and Samaritan do not occur in Mark at all and in Matthew only once, whereas Luke seems to have carried his inquiries into the country and treasured whatever he could find of Christ's words about it.

Give the Hebraism in the opening clause, that the days were fulfilled, and say what period had ended: the time fixed for his being in Galilee, his ministry there finished and the miracles wrought that were to be wrought in those parts. Note that the Samaritans seem to have received the messengers gladly, hoping for miracles and for some approbation of their worship, and to have refused only when Christ came in person on his way to Jerusalem.

Report Bishop Pearce's objection, since it is grammatical and serious: the verb before the word denotes a time completed, which the ascension then was not, so the sense must be that the time was past for retiring from Judea as he had hitherto done, having lived in Galilee lest the Jews should lay hold on him before his ministry was finished. Note that the messengers are literally angels, which proves that the word does not always mean heavenly beings, and that the two were probably James and John. On the refusal, explain the enmity: the Samaritans feared Jehovah and served other gods, and in religious matters had no dealings with the Jews.
State the occasion plainly: the time being near in which he must accomplish his life-giving passion and ascend up to heaven, he determined to go up to Jerusalem.

debates.question: Does 'when the time was come that he should be received up' mean the Ascension, or his withdrawing from Galilee?

sides.position: The Ascension: the word denotes removal from a lower place to a higher and is used elsewhere of that event, and the sacrifice was voluntary, since he would have been safe had he stayed in Galilee
His withdrawing, on the grammatical ground that the preceding verb denotes a time completed, which the ascension then was not
Both: it is called so not only because he was then withdrawn from the midst of men but because, leaving the mean prison of the flesh, he ascended on high

outliers.note: Alone says why the narrative is worth having at all, listing five uses: it shows the divine courage and firmness of Christ in despising death, what deadly enmities differences about religion produce, how headlong human nature is towards impatience, how ready we are to go wrong in imitating the saints, and how his example calls us to meekness.

Alone turns the phrase into a chronological frame, taking the decease to be included in the receiving up and reckoning that from this point Christ resolved to attend every feast preceding it — Tabernacles first, the Dedication some ten weeks later, and at length his own Passover; and alone asks whether Jews would lodge in a Samaritan town at all, answering that nothing but hatred forbade it, since their land and waters and dwellings and roads were reckoned clean.

Alone explains the refusal by the old dispute over the site of the temple, Gerizim against Jerusalem, supposing the Samaritans had hoped Jesus would decide for them; and draws from it that men wish all teachers of religion to fall in with their own views and reject without examination whatever favours a rival.

themes: And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem,
And sent messengers before his face: and they went, and entered into a village of the Samaritans, to make ready for him.
And they did not receive him, because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem.

54.pericope_label: Wilt thou that we command fire; ye know not what spirit ye are of

schools.summary: Set out both ways of construing the rebuke — that the disciples did not know the Spirit given to their Master and promised to them was one of gentleness, or that in yielding to what they took for righteous anger they were yielding to the evil mind at enmity with God — and prefer the first, as agreeing better with what follows, since the Spirit which claimed them led him to save and not to destroy. But do not preach the clause without saying that it is wanting in the best manuscripts, and that the sentence after it is absent from many good ones too; it is at least open to conjecture that they came in from an oral tradition. Note also the two deliberative subjunctives, probably two questions — dost thou wish? shall we bid? — and that the disciples quote the Greek of Kings.

Say who spoke and why they in particular: only the two are meant, and having been the messengers they were the more provoked at the indignity offered to their master. And on the reply, note the manner as well as the matter, that he turned himself about and looked on them and sharply reproved their intemperate zeal, their passion of wrath and anger, and their desire of revenge. Then draw the general rule: whoever undertakes anything ought to be sure he has the authority and guidance of the Spirit, since many are impelled by the warmth of their zeal but, wanting prudence, their ebullitions end in foam; and the examples of the saints are no defence to us unless the same Spirit that directed them dwells in us.

Give the local occasion, since Elisha did the like at or near this very place, which is why the motion was made here rather than after some other affront. Then be exact about the text: the words about the spirit and about the Son of man not coming to destroy are wanting in a long list of manuscripts, Griesbach removes the latter clause, and the most ancient copies probably read simply that he turned and rebuked them, and they went to another village. Whatever is done with the text, the moral stands — vengeance belongs to the Lord, and what we suffer for his sake should be left to him to reprove or punish, the insult being offered to him and not to us.

debates.question: Are the words about the spirit, and about the Son of man not coming to destroy, genuine?

sides.position: Doubtful: the clause about the spirit is wanting in the best manuscripts, and the following sentence in many good ones, perhaps inserted from oral tradition
Very doubtful, and Griesbach removes the latter clause; the most ancient copies probably read only that he turned and rebuked them, and they went to another village
Treated as genuine and made the point of the story, a charge to imitate the Son of man in spirit and temper zeal like his

outliers.note: Alone makes the episode a case study in bad imitation, holding that men plead the example of Elijah without considering how far they differ from him, and that the Samaritans cloaked their idolatry under a pretext just as plausible, so that both parties, neglecting judgement, were apes rather than imitators of the holy fathers.

Alone lists the manuscript authorities against the disputed clauses and reconstructs what the most ancient copies probably read, leaving the narrative to run straight from the rebuke to the departure for another village.
Alone suspects the two of hearing thunder and lightning in their own new name of Boanerges, and supposing it might break out at pleasure.

themes: And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
For the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them. And they went to another village.

57.pericope_label: Foxes have holes; let the dead bury their dead

schools.summary: Note that Matthew omits the call to follow and so makes this man a volunteer, though the two accounts do not really conflict; and that the scribe's father was probably still alive, as in the similar case in Tobit, so that what he meant was that he could not leave a living father to follow Jesus about the country. Set the problem in its general form, since one of the difficulties of life is the relation of duties to each other and which comes first, burial being a sacred duty of long standing. State the paradox plainly: the spiritually dead can bury the literally dead. And supply the idiom from Jewish usage, where the Gentiles were reckoned simply as dead — the people of the earth do not live — and where four sorts were accounted dead even among themselves, the blind, the leprous, the poor and the childless.

Raise the question of where the incident belongs, since the words on both sides are exactly those in Matthew, which makes it look like the same history — though Christ may have been accosted the same way twice and answered alike. And if it is Matthew's account, note that it stood in a different journey altogether and has been inserted here without regard to the order of time.
Reduce the answer about the foxes to a single instruction: first understand the terms, and consider on what conditions you are to follow.
Take the possessive in the reply as decisive: by saying their dead, Christ shows that this man's father was not his dead, the deceased having been, it seems, of the number of the unbelieving.

Hear presumption in the first offer. God is bountiful but does not give heavenly and divine gifts absolutely and indiscriminately, only to those worthy to receive them, who free their souls from the stains of wickedness; and this man's approach shows both tardiness in the coming and too great confidence in the asking, since he sought not simply to follow as others of the people did but caught at the honour of the apostleship — whereas no man takes that honour to himself but he that is called of God.

Face the difficulty squarely rather than explaining it away: burial is a religious duty we have received, so how can the burial even of a father's body be forbidden, unless human things are to be postponed to divine? Answer in terms of attention rather than affection — the employment is good, but the hindrance is greater, for a man who divides his pursuits draws down his affections and a man who divides his care delays his progress, so that what is most important must be set about first; and note that the apostles did the same thing when they ordained others to distribute alms rather than be occupied in it themselves. Then turn the severity forward: if a disciple is reproved for wishing merely to take leave at home, what shall be said of those who for no advantage keep visiting the houses of the people they left behind in the world?

outliers.note: Alone refuses to dissolve the hardness of the saying and instead reconciles it with the duty of burial by an argument about divided attention, that he who divides his pursuits draws down his affections and he who divides his care delays his advance.
Alone rests the interpretation on the possessive pronoun, arguing from their dead that the man's father was not reckoned among Christ's dead and was probably of the number of the unbelieving.

Alone supposes the father still living, on the analogy of a similar case in Tobit, so that the request was not for a funeral but for an indefinite postponement; and alone passes on Plummer's description of the man as one of the casual disciples of whom there are always too many.

themes: And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain man said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
And Jesus said unto him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
And he said unto another, Follow me. But he said, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.
Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.

61.pericope_label: No man having put his hand to the plough and looking back

schools.summary: Note that this third example is peculiar to Luke, and that the offer looks spontaneous while being coupled at once with a plea for delay. Since no father or wife or children is named, it is at least arguable that the man was free of the closer and more binding ties altogether and the plea was therefore hollow. Be careful with him too: the pronoun means simply another rather than one of a different sort, taking leave of one's household was in itself a good thing to do, and the verb is an old military one meaning to detach or to assign as a detachment of soldiers — the trouble being only that he also had something which had to come first.

Say that this is the third person in Luke's account and that Matthew has only two. Then read him as one too strongly attached to the world to be ready: he offers to join the family of Christ, but with a reservation, as men do when preparing for a journey, and that is why the reproof is so severe — professing in words to be a follower, he turned his back until his worldly business was despatched.

Prefer the rendering the Greek supports better, permit me to set my affairs in order at home. On that reading the man had Elisha's case in view, whose identical request Elijah granted; and the refusal turns on the difference between the men, since Christ saw too much attachment to earth here and saw that even a short return to worldly employment was likely to stifle the desires he now felt. State it as a rule: what we plead against the execution of God's designs is sometimes the very thing we ought to disengage from immediately. Then apply the ploughman narrowly, and ask whether anyone engaged in secular employment can properly discharge the work of the ministry, since a man holding the plough cannot keep it straight if he looks behind him, and whoever thinks it necessary to cultivate the favour of the world is not far from betraying the interests of God and his church.

outliers.note: Alone turns the refusal into a rule about counsel, that the purpose to be a Christian requires decision, and that a man should not tamper with the world, nor consult earthly friends about it, nor even allow worldly friends to advise him whether to be a Christian at all. His summary is the flattest sentence in the chapter: religion is everything or nothing, and he who is not willing to sacrifice everything for the cause of God is really willing to sacrifice nothing.

Alone proposes a different rendering of the request — permit me to set my affairs in order at home — and alone applies the ploughman to the ministry specifically, calling a farmer and a minister of the gospel incompatible characters.
Alone infers from the absence of any named father, wife or children that the man may have had no close ties at all, so that the plea for a formal farewell was hollow and unreal.

themes: And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house.
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
